title: The Circles Japan RAL Exposure is a 26″ Rim Brake ATB – John Watson
content:
Cari and John stayed in Japan after the Bespoked Osaka show and have been hanging out with the Circles fam in Nagoya. While there, he documented the newest product from Circles’ in-house outdoor brand, Ride Alive, or RAL for short. The RAL Exposure is a 26″ steel rim brake ATB, designed for commuting and mixed terrain riding. Let’s check out this $500 frameset below!

Circles is a shop based in Nagoya, Japan. Ten years ago, I did an in-depth Shop Visit on the multi-faceted culture surrounding the bike shop, including its brands Sim Works and RAL, or Ride Alive. Since it’s both The Radavist’s and Circles’ 20th anniversary, boss man Shinya flew Cari and me out to document the Bespoked show and to check out what Circles has been up to over the past ten years.

The short answer is a lot. So much that you’ll have to wait to see the updates, but I wanted to share something special from RAL today.

RAL Exposure Quick Hits

  • ~$500 frameset (varies due to currency conversion)
  • Made in Taiwan by Maxway
  • Three Sizes: S, M, L
  • Rim brake only
  • Single-speed optimized, but modular dropout design allows for a derailleur hanger
  • Gray Card paint color
  • 26 x 2.6″ clearance
  • Fender mounts
  • 1 1/8″ steerer
  • BSA BB

Circles Customer

After a week of Bespoked Osaka coverage and all the high-end custom bikes from the show, it felt fitting to share a $500 frameset. Japanese bicycle commuting culture is primarily mamachari bikes. Cruisers with low saddles, baskets, racks, and a kid’s seat. Other than that, most people just ride their road or gravel bikes to work.

In the previous decade, vintage mountain bikes have become popular in Japan. Customers of Circles will build them into commuters and campers, designed to haul work items during the week and camping stuff on the weekends. An increasing number of Circles customers have gotten interested in the post-performance cycling space and have requested a more affordable bike than the Sim Works Doppo line.

The problem with vintage mountain bikes is they don’t fit a big tire, and it’s sometimes hard to find the right size for a rider. This prompted Shinya and Masashi from Circles and RAL to design a bicycle for entry-level riders, inspired by vintage mountain bikes.

Exposure Model

This new bike, dubbed the RAL Exposure, named after photography exposure, is a simple, 26″ wheeled, rim-braked, single-speed commuter, designed for fenders, racks, a 1 1/8″ steerer, but with clearance for 2.6″ tires. It comes in Gray Card grey, a template used to establish the correct white balance in photography, and has replaceable single-speed dropouts that can be adapted to use a derailleur hanger as well.

Most of the RAL Exposures being built by Circles are flat bar and single-speed, but they have built a few drop-bar bikes as well as a number of bikes with gears. To keep the price point low, the Exposure frame is made in Taiwan by Maxway, and it lacks any cable guides for a rear mech. These frames are more robust than the 1″ quill bikes of the 1980s and have clean, elegant lines. Shinya and Masashi’s eye for design shines through in such a simple chassis.

Ryoma’s RAL Exposure

I photographed Ryoma Nakamoto’s personal single-speed, flat bar Exposure as well as a drop-bar build spec for the Circles showroom floor. Ryoma is an engineer at Sim Works, but he started in the shipping and distribution department while he was in school.

He built his up for commuting – fenders coming now that the rainy season is here – with used components. He splurged on nice Sim Works Homage tires, custom Sim Works Standalone rims, laced to Deore hubs and Hunter Smooth Move handlebars. With a Sim Works Sim Heads headset.

Dirt Drop Exposure

For the drop-bar option, Circles poached a drivetrain from Masashi’s MB-1 and utilized a Velo Orange Cigne stem to get the bars nice and high, just like a legit dirt drop bike from the 1980s. The RAL H2O Saddle is a throwback to 1980s designs. A Rivendell Silver shifter is mounted to the drop bar clamp area to shift the mech. Because Circles wanted to keep the bike as simple and as affordable as possible, there are no cable guides for a derailleur, but you can use any number of aftermarket clamps or zip ties to run the cables.

Affordable but Not Heavy

What was most shocking to me was how light the frame is. I was expecting it to be a heavy bike, but it was surprisingly light. It comes in sub-5 lbs for the largest size, or around 2,240 grams for the frame and 1,110 g (2.4 lbs) for the fork. All for around $500 USD for a frame and fork.

Circles in Japan has these frames, which they will ship internationally, and Sim Works USA should be stocking them soon, too.

Arigato to Shinya, Masashi, Ryoma, and the Circles fam for having us in Nagoya! More to come…
